verses.text: This is Yahweh’s word that came to Jeremiah concerning the drought.
“Judah mourns, and its gates languish, they sit in black on the ground; and the cry of Jerusalem goes up.
Their nobles send their little ones to the waters. They come to the cisterns, and find no water. They return with their vessels empty. They are disappointed and confounded, and cover their heads.
Because of the ground which is cracked, because no rain has been in the land. The plowmen are disappointed. They cover their heads.
Yes, the hind also in the field calves, and forsakes her young, because there is no grass.
The wild donkeys stand on the bare heights. They pant for air like jackals. Their eyes fail, because there is no vegetation.
Though our iniquities testify against us, work for your name’s sake, Yahweh; for our rebellions are many. We have sinned against you.
You hope of Israel, its Savior in the time of trouble, why should you be as a foreigner in the land, and as a wayfaring man who turns aside to stay for a night?
Why should you be like a scared man, as a mighty man who can’t save? Yet you, Yahweh, are in the middle of us, and we are called by your name. Don’t leave us.

Yahweh says to this people, “Even so they have loved to wander. They have not restrained their feet. Therefore Yahweh does not accept them. Now he will remember their iniquity, and punish them for their sins.”
Yahweh said to me, “Don’t pray for this people for their good.

When they fast, I will not hear their cry; and when they offer burnt offering and meal offering, I will not accept them; but I will consume them by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence.”
Then I said, “Ah, Lord Yahweh! Behold, the prophets tell them, ‘You will not see the sword, neither shall you have famine; but I will give you assured peace in this place.’”

Then Yahweh said to me, “The prophets prophesy lies in my name. I didn’t send them, neither have I commanded them, neither did I speak to them. They prophesy to you a lying vision, divination, and a thing of nothing, and the deceit of their own heart.

Therefore Yahweh says concerning the prophets who prophesy in my name, and I didn’t send them, yet they say, ‘Sword and famine will not be in this land.’ Those prophets will be consumed by sword and famine.

The people to whom they prophesy shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem because of the famine and the sword. They shall have no one to bury them — them, their wives, nor their sons, nor their daughters: for I will pour their wickedness on them.

“You shall say this word to them, “‘Let my eyes run down with tears night and day, and let them not cease; for the virgin daughter of my people is broken with a great breach, with a very grievous wound.

If I go out into the field, then, behold, the slain with the sword! If I enter into the city, then, behold, those who are sick with famine! For both the prophet and the priest go about in the land, and have no knowledge.’”

Have you utterly rejected Judah? Has your soul loathed Zion? Why have you struck us, and there is no healing for us? We looked for peace, but no good came; and for a time of healing, and behold, dismay!
We acknowledge, Yahweh, our wickedness, and the iniquity of our fathers; for we have sinned against you.
Do not abhor us, for your name’s sake. Do not disgrace the throne of your glory. Remember, and don’t break your covenant with us.
Are there any among the vanities of the nations that can cause rain? Or can the sky give showers? Aren’t you he, Yahweh our God? Therefore we will wait for you; for you have made all these things.

footnotes.content: When drought comes, it speaks louder than any sermon. God's word often arrives not as comfortable whisper but as hard reality—the prophet must read it in the land's own suffering. Here Jeremiah learns that famine is the canvas on which the Lord writes His message.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice how sorrow takes the city: gates grow weak, nobles sit wrapped in black. It is the posture of a people who have finally fallen silent before God. Sometimes we must be brought low before we can truly listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The servants sent by nobles find no water at the cisterns—even the household's servants know emptiness. When thirst becomes universal, no rank can escape it. Both master and servant discover together that life depends on what only heaven can give.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The plowman's disappointment cuts deepest—he prepares the ground in faith, yet earth cracks beneath his hands. There is a loneliness in working faithfully when the heavens refuse to answer. Yet even this silence teaches us to look upward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the hind—a creature of instinct and fierce love for her young—must abandon them. This is how severe the drought has become: nature itself breaks its most sacred bonds. When creation groans, we glimpse how deeply God's judgment reaches.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wild donkeys on barren heights, eyes failing, panting like jackals. The hunter becomes as desperate as the hunted. In extremity, all creatures stand equal before need, and all must turn their gaze toward sky and hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah owns the people's sin with them: 'our iniquities,' 'we have sinned.' He doesn't stand apart pleading their case but stands within their guilt. This is intercession—not excusing the people, but weeping with them before the throne of grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The 'Hope of Israel' is the ancient name for the Lord—yet here He is addressed as if a stranger passing through. How can salvation itself seem like a foreigner? This is the deepest pain of judgment: to feel abandoned by the One whose name means we belong to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Yet you, Yahweh, are in the middle of us'—even in the shadow, faith reaches for the truth that God has not left. The prayer holds both the pain of abandonment and the stubborn knowledge that His name is still upon us. This is the wrestling of trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people have 'loved to wander,' not forced but chosen. There is something in human nature that keeps running from home even when home is mercy itself. God's patience is not indifference—He remembers, He counts, and He responds with justice because He loves the truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The command 'Don't pray for this people' is shocking—prayer itself is forbidden. Yet this is not cruelty but clarity: sometimes the Lord removes the intercessor's own prayer to show that the door of repentance belongs only to those who truly turn. Silence can be its own mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even their ritual fasting and offerings cannot reach Him now. Sin has put distance between heaven and earth that no outward act can bridge. Only a turned heart can. Sometimes the Lord must withdraw the comfort of ceremony to teach us that He wants us, not our performances.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah knows what the false prophets are saying: 'You will have peace.' He has heard their comfort. The hardest part of faithfulness is speaking the hard word while others around you promise ease. The prophet's loneliness lies in knowing the truth no one wants to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: False prophets claim authority from the Lord but speak 'lying vision,' making up comfort from their own hearts. The test of a prophet is not popularity but fidelity to the hard word. Truth and mercy belong to God alone; we mistake our own desires for His voice at terrible cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those who prophesy lies in His name will themselves be consumed by the very judgment they denied. There is a justice here: the prophet who promises 'no sword, no famine' will know both. Words matter—they shape what we believe, and belief shapes how we prepare.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Cast out in the streets with no one to bury them—the final indignity. In ancient understanding, burial meant rest, memory, belonging to the people. To lie unburied was to be forgotten by God and man alike. This is judgment at its most complete.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prophet is commanded to weep—'Let my eyes run down with tears night and day.' This is his office: to feel what the people cannot yet feel, to grieve before they grieve, to stand in the gap with his tears. A prophet without a broken heart is not truly speaking for God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Prophet and priest alike wander 'without knowledge'—the very leaders who should see God's hand have become blind. Spiritual leadership that rests on comfort rather than truth cannot survive hard times. Only those anchored in reality can guide others through what is coming.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prayer moves from statement to question: 'Have you utterly rejected Judah?' We look for peace and find dismay instead. Abandonment is the deepest question of the faithful—not 'Why do I suffer?' but 'Have you forgotten me?' Yet even this question is prayer, a reaching toward God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the confession comes: 'We acknowledge our wickedness.' It took the fullness of drought to bring the people to this honest word. True confession does not excuse or minimize but owns the sin plainly. Only in such acknowledgment can restoration begin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Remember, and don't break your covenant'—the prayer rests on covenant promise, not on the people's worthiness. It is an appeal not to justice but to the faithfulness of God's own word and name. Even in judgment, the remnant clings to the word He once gave.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Looking back from a later road, we hear an echo in this question: 'Aren't you he, Yahweh our God?' Every generation rediscovers this dependence. Rain comes from heaven alone; crops come from heaven alone; mercy comes from heaven alone. Readers today hear an echo in a world that forgets where its provision truly flows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
